subskill: Integer optimum: tied plans for the most items
prompt:
A shipping crate can hold a total mass of at most 133 kilograms and a total volume of at most 179 liters. It will be packed with boxes of two types, P and Q, described in the table below.
Box type | Mass (kilograms) | Volume (liters)
P | 9 | 13
Q | 10 | 11
Only whole boxes are packed. The crate is to hold as many boxes as possible in total. How many different combinations of type P and type Q boxes achieve this?
explanation: Let p and q be the numbers of type P and type Q boxes. The crate requires 9p + 10q ≤ 133 and 13p + 11q ≤ 179, and the goal is to make p + q as large as possible. The two boundary lines meet at p ≈ 10.55, q ≈ 3.81, where p + q ≈ 14.35, so no plan can hold 15 boxes. Rounding the corner down gives (10, 3), only 13 boxes, so the best whole-number plans have to be found directly: test p + q = 14. Mass requires 9p + 10(14 - p) ≤ 133, so 140 - p ≤ 133 and p ≥ 7. Volume requires 13p + 11(14 - p) ≤ 179, so 2p + 154 ≤ 179 and p ≤ 12.5, so p ≤ 12. Thus p = 7, 8, 9, 10, 11 or 12, giving (7, 7), (8, 6), (9, 5), (10, 4), (11, 3) and (12, 2): 6 combinations. Choice 1 treats the rounded corner as the single best plan without checking which other combinations reach the greatest total. Choice 8 swaps the masses of the two box types (10 kilograms for P and 9 for Q), which changes the mass bound and the count. Choice 13 counts the 14-box combinations that satisfy the volume limit (p ≤ 12) but never checks the mass limit.
solve: const ok=(x,y)=>9*x+10*y<=133&&13*x+11*y<=179;let best=-1,n=0;for(let x=0;x<=40;x++)for(let y=0;y<=40;y++)if(ok(x,y)){const v=x+y;if(v>best){best=v;n=1}else if(v===best)n++}return n

distractor_solve.8: const ok=(x,y)=>10*x+9*y<=133&&13*x+11*y<=179;let best=-1,n=0;for(let x=0;x<=40;x++)for(let y=0;y<=40;y++)if(ok(x,y)){const v=x+y;if(v>best){best=v;n=1}else if(v===best)n++}return n
distractor_solve.13: const ok=(x,y)=>9*x+10*y<=133&&13*x+11*y<=179;let best=-1;for(let x=0;x<=40;x++)for(let y=0;y<=40;y++)if(ok(x,y))best=Math.max(best,x+y);let n=0;for(let x=0;x<=best;x++){const y=best-x;if(13*x+11*y<=179)n++}return n

mechanism: two caps meet at a non-lattice corner (p + q about 14.4)
rounded corner gives only 13, so test the level p + q = 14
each cap turns into a bound on p along the level line
count the integers between the two bounds
quantity_asked: number of whole-number combinations that hold the greatest total number of boxes

setup.i: mass cap and volume cap given in a table, two box types
setup.ii: total number of boxes (unweighted x + y) as large as possible; several lattice plans tie
setup.iii: number of combinations that hold the most boxes

plugback.why: Ascending, a student tries 1 and then 6. Neither can be checked by substitution: an option is a count, not a plan, so testing it means finding the greatest whole-number total (14, which the rounded corner's 13 does not show) and then counting every combination at that total against both caps, which is the whole solution.

1.why: Rounds the corner (10.55, 3.81) to a whole-number plan and reports it as the single best plan; the stem does not say whether the best total is shared, so nothing marks a lone plan as too few.

8.why: Reads the mass column against the wrong box type (P 10 kg, Q 9 kg); the swapped mass bound lets more combinations through, and the stem gives no hint whether a misread table raises or lowers the count.

13.why: Finds the right greatest total, 14, but checks the 14-box combinations against the volume limit only; the student cannot tell from the stem how many combinations either limit removes.

intermediate_check: 1: no - 1 is a plan count from the rounded corner; no printed relation turns it into 6. 8: no - a count under a swapped table; no printed rate maps 8 to 6. 13: no - the count with the mass check left out; reaching 6 from 13 needs the mass bound p ≥ 7 worked out, not one printed relation.
shape_check: The stem hands over: the answer is a positive whole number (at least one combination fits), and the combinations at the best total form a run of consecutive p values. All four options are positive whole numbers; parity is not forced (1, 13 odd; 6, 8 even). All four survive together.
interior_parity_check: Middle values 6 and 8: both one-digit whole numbers, same display form and complexity; the key 6 is not cleaner than 8.
arith_class_check: Key 6 is even, as is 8; 1 and 13 are odd. 6 is not alone in any class the stem implies (no multiple-of or roundness condition).

idea_probe.nearest: 40fba632-b25 (live v26 D1, from the extra search 'how many different&combinations'): its count comes from an objective exactly parallel to the budget with two minimums. Here the objective is the plain total p + q, parallel to neither cap, the tie is a run of lattice points on the level p + q = 14 cut by both caps, and the data come from a table. ALG-H3-07 (prior) counts solutions of one exact linear equation, not an optimum.

self_audit.note: Covering the work, how many options remain legal from the stem alone? All four: each is a positive whole-number count; the level p + q = 14 holds 15 whole-number combinations before either cap is applied, so even 13 is not ruled out by size. Could a student confirm an option against the stem in one routine step (key at try 2)? No: an option is a count, and checking it needs the top total 14 (above the rounded corner's 13) plus the two bounds on p, which is the full solution; trying 1 first does not help because no plan is offered to substitute. Is the bypass option really what skipping THIS item's decision point gives? Yes: a student who rounds the real corner and treats that plan as the optimum answers 1 combination; the bypass sits below the key here, balancing D1/D4 where it sits above. No option is a sum, difference or mean of two others (1 + 6 = 7, 8 - 6 = 2, 13 - 8 = 5, 13 - 6 = 7, 13 - 1 = 12; none an option). Preflight (read) lines: DPAIR 6 + 8 = 14 = 13 + 1 and DPAIR/DSUM 6 + 13 = 19 = 9 + 10 are coincidences of the printed masses and volumes; no stem reading adds them to move between counts.
